blocks.prompt: The Devil That Screams in the Dark
blocks.text: The Tasmanian devil lives on one island. That island is Tasmania, near Australia. It is the biggest meat eating animal with a pouch. A devil sleeps all day in a hollow log. When the sun goes down, it comes out to eat. Devils are loud. They screech and growl and sneeze at each other over dinner. Long ago, people heard that noise in the dark and named the animal a devil. But a devil does not want to fight you. When it gets scared, it opens its mouth wide and yawns. The yawn looks mean. It really means please go away.

blocks.prompt: The Cleaning Crew of Tasmania
blocks.text: Every night on the island of Tasmania, something black and low to the ground goes looking for dinner. It is a Tasmanian devil, and it is about the size of a small dog. The devil does not do much hunting. Mostly it finds animals that are already dead, and that turns out to be a useful job. A dead wallaby left lying in the sun would fill up with flies. A devil cleans it away. When a devil eats, it eats everything. Meat, fur, and bone all go down. For its size, a devil has one of the strongest bites of any animal alive. Those flat back teeth crack bones the way you might crack a nut. The noise is the part people remember. Devils gather around one dead animal, and they screech and cough and growl at each other in the dark. Hundreds of years ago, settlers heard that sound and decided only a devil could make it. The name stuck. The animal is really rather shy. If you walked up to one, it would most likely run.

notes: A marsupial, like kangaroos and koalas

Largest meat eating marsupial on Earth

blocks.prompt: Rice-Grain Babies and a Backward Pouch
blocks.text: The Tasmanian devil is a marsupial, which means its babies finish growing outside the womb, inside a pouch. Kangaroos do this. So do koalas and possums. But a devil's pouch has a twist: it opens backward, toward the mother's tail. A devil spends its nights digging in dirt and shoving its head inside dead animals, and a forward facing pouch would pack full of grit. Backward, the babies stay clean. What happens inside that pouch is harder to think about. A mother devil can give birth to as many as thirty young at once, each one about the size of a grain of rice, pink and blind and no bigger than your fingernail. They must crawl up her belly and into the pouch on their own. Inside the pouch there are only four teats. The first four to arrive latch on and stay. The rest do not survive. Those four are called joeys, and they hang on for about four months. When they finally let go, they ride on their mother's back or wait in a den while she goes out to feed. By around nine months they are living on their own. A wild devil is lucky to reach five years old. In that short life it will scream at rivals, crack bones with the strongest bite for its size of any mammal alive, and clean up the dead animals nobody else wants. It is a hard living, and the devil is built for it.

notes: Sarcophilus harrisii
Devil Facial Tumor Disease found in 1996
A cancer spread by biting, not a virus
Wild numbers fell by about eighty percent
Devils now breed a year earlier than they used to
Returned to mainland Australia in 2020

blocks.prompt: The Cancer That Learned to Travel
blocks.text: For most of its history the Tasmanian devil had one real problem: other Tasmanian devils. Devils squabble over carcasses. They bite each other on the face, they screech, they sneeze at one another, and then they go back to eating. The wounds heal. This has worked for thousands of years. In 1996 a wildlife photographer in the northeast of Tasmania took a picture of a devil with a strange lumpy growth on its face. Nobody knew it at the time, but that photograph was the start of one of the strangest disease stories in biology. Cancer is not supposed to be contagious. A tumor grows from one animal's own cells, and it dies when that animal dies. Devil Facial Tumor Disease broke the rule. The tumor itself is the infection. When one devil bites another's face, living cancer cells come loose and take root in the fresh wound. Every facial tumor on every sick devil in Tasmania is descended from a single animal that died decades ago. Her cells never stopped dividing. They simply changed hosts. The disease crossed the island in about twenty years. Devil numbers fell by roughly eighty percent, and in some places by far more. A devil that catches it usually dies within months, and it dies young, often before it has raised a litter. Then something unexpected happened. Devils started breeding earlier. Females that once had their first litter at two years old began having them at one, slipping a generation in ahead of the disease. Researchers have also found signs of rapid change in devil genes in the regions that handle immune response, which suggests some devils are now surviving what killed their parents. A few tumors have even been seen to shrink and disappear on their own. The devil is not saved. It is also not finished. People are working alongside it. Healthy devils are kept in insurance populations, and in 2020 a group was released into a fenced sanctuary at Barrington Tops in New South Wales, putting wild devils back on mainland Australia for the first time in roughly three thousand years.

notes: Sarcophilus harrisii: roughly, Harris's meat lover
Largest carnivorous marsupial since the thylacine died in 1936
Eats up to forty percent of its body weight at one sitting
Two separate transmissible cancers: DFTD and DFT2
Gone from mainland Australia for about 3,000 years
Returned to a fenced mainland sanctuary in 2020

blocks.prompt: The Devil, the Dead, and the Cancer That Travels
blocks.text: Sarcophilus harrisii translates, roughly, as Harris's meat lover, and the name is fair. The Tasmanian devil is the largest carnivorous marsupial left on Earth, a title it inherited in 1936, when the last thylacine died in a Hobart zoo. A big male weighs up to about twenty-six pounds and stands no higher than your knee. He is black, blunt faced, and built like a barrel on short legs. He is also, by most measures, the noisiest animal in Australia. The name came from the noise. European settlers in Tasmania heard screeching and coughing and low growling out in the dark bush and concluded that whatever made it could not be an ordinary animal. They were wrong twice over. The devil is ordinary, and the racket is mostly bluff. Devils crowding a carcass insult each other rather than truly fight, because a real fight risks a wound, and a wound is expensive. The famous wide open gape that looks like fury is not a threat at all. It is a sign of fear and uncertainty. The devil is telling you it is nervous. What the devil does for a living deserves more respect than it gets. It is mainly a scavenger. It locates a dead wallaby by smell, sometimes from over half a mile away, and then it eats the whole animal: muscle, organs, fur, and bone. Its jaws deliver one of the strongest bites, relative to body size, of any mammal alive, and its back teeth work like bolt cutters. A devil can put away forty percent of its own body weight in a single sitting. Wherever devils are common, carcasses vanish quickly, blowflies have nowhere to breed, and feral cats and foxes find the island a harder place to make a living. The devil is Tasmania's cleaning crew, and it is unpaid. Then came 1996. A photographer working in the northeast of the island took a picture of a devil with a lumpy growth spilling from its jaw. Within a few years that growth had a name, Devil Facial Tumor Disease, and a disturbing explanation. Cancer, as a rule, is not contagious. A tumor is built from one body's own broken cells, and it dies with that body. This one does not. The tumor cells themselves are the infection. When devils bite each other's faces, as devils constantly do, cancer cells transfer into the fresh wound and grow there. Every facial tumor in Tasmania is a living piece of one devil, a female who died in the 1990s. Her cells never stopped dividing. They simply changed hosts. Only a handful of transmissible cancers are known anywhere in nature, and the devil has the bad luck to carry two of them. A second, separate line, called DFT2, turned up in southern Tasmania in 2014, this one descended from a male. Together they have cut the wild population by roughly eighty percent. The interesting part is what the devils did about it. Under that pressure, females that used to breed first at two years old began breeding at one, squeezing a generation in ahead of the disease. Genome studies have found signs of rapid selection in immune related regions, and in some long infected areas devils have been found with tumors that shrink away on their own. Evolution is running in real time, in an animal with a five year lifespan, and it can be measured. People are running alongside it. Disease free devils are held in insurance populations, and in 2020 conservationists released a group into a fenced sanctuary at Barrington Tops in New South Wales, putting wild devils back on mainland Australia for the first time in roughly three thousand years, since dingoes and a changing climate pushed them off it. Whether the devil holds on by its own strength is still an open question. It is worth noticing that the animal named for its scream is being undone by something completely silent.
